The lithosphere is Earth's rigid outer shell, broken into a mosaic of tectonic plates. These plates float on the asthenosphere, a ductile layer beneath them that can flow slowly.
Three forces drive plate motion: mantle convection, slab pull, and ridge push. Relative motion between plates is measured in centimetres per year (cm yr⁻¹).

Why do earthquakes cluster at boundaries rather than scatter? The key point: earthquakes are not randomly distributed; they trace the kinematic framework of plate interactions. Their pattern maps where and how plates interact.

## Types of Plate Boundaries

## Plate Speeds in Practice
Plate speeds are measured as rates, in centimetres per year. The material gives two worked values: the Pacific Plate moves northwest relative to the North American Plate at about 5 cm yr⁻¹, and the Nazca Plate subducts beneath South America at about 8 cm yr⁻¹.
Why the rates matter: these fast motions explain the high frequency of large earthquakes along the Circum-Pacific 'Ring of Fire.' Faster convergence means strain is stored and released more often.
Depth follows plate setting. Shallow events, at 10 km or less, dominate divergent ridges and transform faults. Intermediate to deep events, 30–300 km, occur in the Wadati-Benioff zone of subducting slabs.
A typical subduction earthquake at 30 km depth releases energy from two sources at once: crustal bending and slab dehydration.
The seismic cycle at a convergent margin has four stages. Interseismic: the locked zone accumulates strain over decades to centuries. Coseismic: sudden slip releases stored elastic energy in seconds to minutes. Postseismic: afterslip and viscoelastic relaxation redistribute stress over months to years. Preseismic: possible precursory signals such as foreshocks and slow slip.
Hazard assessment applies all of this. Seismic gap theory holds that segments which have not ruptured in a full cycle are candidates for future large events. GPS and InSAR monitor plate-scale velocities in cm yr⁻¹ to refine coupling models.

Takeaway: strain builds slowly, releases suddenly, then relaxes — with possible warning signals before the release.

## Seismic Gaps and Geodetic Monitoring
Seismic gap theory: a fault segment that has not ruptured through a full earthquake cycle has not released its stored strain. Such a segment is therefore a candidate for a future large event.
The seismic cycle at a convergent margin runs: interseismic (locked zone accumulates strain, decades to centuries) → coseismic (sudden slip releases elastic energy, seconds to minutes) → postseismic (afterslip and viscoelastic relaxation, months to years), with possible preseismic precursors such as foreshocks and slow slip.
GPS and InSAR monitor plate-scale velocities in cm yr⁻¹, refining models of how strongly the plate interface is coupled. Rates matter: the Nazca Plate subducts beneath South America at ≈ 8 cm yr⁻¹, and the Pacific Plate moves ≈ 5 cm yr⁻¹ relative to North America, explaining frequent large earthquakes on the Ring of Fire.
Depth is diagnostic: shallow events (≤ 10 km) dominate ridges and transform faults, while intermediate–deep events (30–300 km) occur in the Wadati–Benioff zone of subducting slabs; a 30 km subduction earthquake releases energy from both crustal bending and slab dehydration.

## Hazard Evaluation Workflow
Hazard evaluation follows a fixed four-step workflow. Step 1: identify the plate boundary type for the region of interest.
Step 2: obtain relative plate velocities (cm yr⁻¹) from global models such as MORVEL or NUVEL-1A.
Step 3: map earthquake depths (km) to infer the seismogenic thickness. Depth distribution of seismicity informs the likely rupture extent and tsunami potential.
Step 4: evaluate coupling and seismic gap status for probabilistic hazard.

Nothing here is scored; read the short lesson, then try the practice questions at your own pace.
The lithosphere is broken into a mosaic of rigid tectonic plates that float on the ductile asthenosphere. Think of it like a knitted blanket laid over soft foam: the stiff fabric pieces (plates) glide over the yielding layer below (asthenosphere).
Plates move because of mantle convection, slab pull, and ridge push. Their relative motion is measured in centimetres per year (cm yr⁻¹).
Boundary types: Divergent | plates pull apart | normal-fault, shallow Convergent | plates collide | thrust-fault, deep to shallow Transform | plates slide past | strike-slip, shallow to intermediate
Earthquakes cluster at boundaries for four reasons: stress accumulation (locked edges build strain past rock strength), fault geometry (old faults concentrate slip), rheological contrast (cold brittle rock beside warm ductile mantle), and geometric incompatibility (curved margins force shear zones).
Key point: earthquakes are not randomly distributed; they trace the kinematic framework of plate interactions. In other words, where plates meet is where quakes happen.

## Earthquake Depths and the Seismic Cycle
Nothing here is scored; these are practice questions, so you can work at your own pace. The material gives two plate speeds: the Pacific Plate moves northwest relative to the North American Plate at about 5 cm per year, and the Nazca Plate subducts beneath South America at about 8 cm per year. These rates explain why large earthquakes are frequent along the Circum-Pacific 'Ring of Fire'. Think of it like a speedrun route: the faster the plate moves, the more often the same stretch of the run (a fault segment) reaches its next big moment.
Earthquake depth tells you the plate setting. Shallow events, at 10 km depth or less, dominate divergent ridges and transform faults. Intermediate to deep events, from 30 to 300 km, occur in the Wadati-Benioff zone, the zone inside a subducting slab. A typical subduction earthquake at 30 km depth releases energy from both crustal bending and slab dehydration.
The seismic cycle at a convergent margin has stages. In the interseismic stage, a locked zone accumulates strain over decades to centuries. In the coseismic stage, sudden slip releases the stored elastic energy in seconds to minutes. In the postseismic stage, afterslip and viscoelastic relaxation redistribute stress over months to years. A preseismic stage may show precursory signals such as foreshocks or slow slip.
In words: strain builds slowly, then one sudden slip empties the store. In a picture: interseismic (decades–centuries) → strain accumulates ↓ coseismic (seconds–minutes) → sudden slip ↓ postseismic (months–years) → stress redistributed (preseismic: foreshocks, slow slip)
Restated once more: depth sorts the plate setting, and the cycle sorts the timing. For hazard work, seismic gap theory says segments that have not ruptured in a full cycle are candidates for future large events. GPS and InSAR monitor plate-scale velocities in cm per year to refine coupling models. Think of it like tracking a knitting project: the unworked segment of the pattern is the one you know still needs its turn.
